<reason>A genuinely high-quality debate where both sides were sharp, disciplined, and well-grounded. A built a compelling case (the veto-holding aggressor makes the collective path illusory; indefinite custody is confiscation without trial; the endpoint dilemma was the debate's best question). But B won the decisive exchanges. B turned A's Iraq precedent in the opening, answered "the collective path does not exist" with the Algiers Accords and successor-state settlements, threaded A's dilemma with "custody conditioned on conduct" (neither return-with-interest nor taking), and defended the reversibility distinction against A's "the shock is already spent" — backed by the observable fact that custodians skim windfall income yet refuse to touch principal. Most decisively, B dismantled A's answer to the symmetry pressure question: A claimed mirror judgments would not be recognized abroad, but B showed recognition is irrelevant because retaliation operates on assets already inside the mirror jurisdiction. A's closing crystallization was excellent, but it rested on a frame B had already partially defused (windfall income reaches victims now; leverage has historically bought signatures). B answered both pressure questions directly with clean A1/A2 structure and kept one coherent line — reversibility — running through every speech. Clipped turns on both sides roughly cancel.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answer on mirror courts: A had answered the symmetry question by arguing third jurisdictions would refuse to recognize an aggressor's retaliatory judgment, but B pointed out that mirror courts need no recognition at all — investors' assets already sit inside their jurisdiction, so "the boomerang acts entirely at home." That gutted A's defense on the round's sharpest pressure question. Runner-up: B's opening turn of the Iraq UNCC precedent (multilateral, consent-based, oil-levy funded — the opposite of unilateral judicial liquidation).</best_rebuttal>
